title: Fish and Chips
subtitle: Beer-battered cod and thick-cut fried chips
excerpt: The British national dish: thick cod fillets in a crisp, golden beer batter alongside fat, fluffy chips. The batter must be ice-cold, the oil must be at the right temperature, and the fish must be drained properly to stay crisp.

recipe.sourceNotes: Fish and chips emerged as Britain's first national takeaway food in the 1860s, when the convergence of the rail network (which brought fresh fish to inland cities) and the widespread adoption of frying in batter produced a cheap, filling, and portable meal that fed the industrial working class. The first documented fish-and-chip shop in England is attributed to John Lees in Mossley, Lancashire, around 1863, though shops in London's East End claim an equal antiquity. The dish spread rapidly: by 1910 there were an estimated 25,000 fish and chip shops in Britain, and by the 1920s it was the most commonly eaten dish in the country. The combination of battered fish and deep-fried potatoes reflects both the Northern European tradition of frying in batter and the Jewish culinary influence brought by Sephardic immigrants to London, who introduced the technique of frying fish in batter.

recipeTools.notes: A large, deep, heavy saucepan for frying; or a deep-fat fryer if available.

content.text: Keep the batter ice-cold: a cold batter hitting hot oil creates steam that makes the batter puff and crisp. A warm batter absorbs oil and turns greasy. Use sparkling water or cold beer instead of flat water, as the CO2 also contributes to the lightness. Fry the chips twice: once at a lower temperature to cook through, then again at a higher temperature to crisp. Oil must be at 180 C for the batter and 190 C for the final chip fry.

items.preparation: thick, skin-off, about 180 g each; patted dry
peeled and cut into chips about 1.5 cm thick
for the batter, plus extra for dusting the fish

content.text: Parboil the chips: cook in salted boiling water for 4 minutes, then drain and leave to steam-dry completely in a colander. This is essential for a fluffy interior. Heat the oil to 150 C in a large deep saucepan. Fry the chips in batches for 4 minutes until cooked through but not yet coloured. Drain on kitchen paper. The oil can be held at 150 C until the batter is ready.

Make the batter: whisk the flour, baking powder, and salt in a bowl. Make a well in the centre and add about 300 ml of ice-cold sparkling water or cold lager, whisking to a smooth, thick-cream consistency. The batter should coat the back of a spoon. Refrigerate until needed.

Raise the oil temperature to 180 C. Dust each cod fillet lightly in plain flour, shaking off the excess, then dip in the batter to coat completely. Lower the fish carefully into the oil, one or two at a time. Fry for 6 to 8 minutes, turning once, until deeply golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper.

Raise the oil to 190 C and fry the chips again in batches for 2 to 3 minutes until golden and very crisp. Season immediately with salt. Serve the fish and chips together with malt vinegar and mushy peas alongside.
